questions.q: What problem does a load balancer solve?
options: Translating domain names to addresses
Letting one server handle more traffic than it could alone, and surviving a server failure
Encrypting traffic between client and server
Assigning private IP addresses to new devices
questions.explain: A load balancer distributes traffic across a pool of servers, letting the system handle more load and survive a single server's failure.

questions.q: What does a health check let a load balancer do?
options: Encrypt traffic to backend servers
Automatically remove an unresponsive backend server from rotation
Assign a backend server's IP address
Translate a domain name to an address
questions.explain: Health checks let the load balancer detect a failing backend and stop sending it traffic automatically, without manual intervention.

questions.q: Which balancing algorithm routes a given client's requests to the same backend server every time?
options: Round robin
Least connections
IP hash
Random selection
questions.explain: IP hash routes based on the client's address, so the same client consistently lands on the same backend server.

options: A device that assigns private IP addresses on a LAN
A server that forwards client requests to one or more backends, often doing more than balancing load
A tool that only works with DNS queries
A rule that blocks unsolicited inbound connections
questions.explain: A reverse proxy forwards requests to backend servers and can also terminate TLS, cache responses, or rewrite URLs — more than balancing load alone.

questions.q: From a shopper's point of view, how many addresses does a load-balanced site appear to have?
options: One for every backend server
Just one — the load balancer's own address
None; it must be accessed by IP only
One per balancing algorithm
questions.explain: The load balancer is the single, stable point every connection hits; backend servers can change behind it without the client ever noticing.
